case_text: Complaint record: A hospital reports that a patient was found unresponsive in bed while connected to a bedside pulse oximeter. The device was not alarming, its display showed dashes instead of values, and the nurse call and alarm systems were not activated. The patient died.

Nurse manager here. We found a patient unresponsive in bed and the pulse ox wasn't alarming at all, just dashes on the screen, and nothing went to the nurse call system. The patient passed away. We need to know what happened with this monitor.
Hosp report: pt found unresponsive in bed. Bedside pulse ox not alarming, display dashes, nurse call/alarm not activated. Pt expired.

The patient died. The hospital's risk team, which filed this during a busy week of accreditation prep, says the patient was found unresponsive in bed while on a bedside pulse oximeter. The display showed dashes rather than numbers, the device was not alarming, and neither the nurse call nor the alarm system activated. The unit sits on a rolling stand.

Sad outcome, but dashes on the display usually just mean the sensor came off, so this is probably a placement issue rather than our device: patient found unresponsive in bed, pulse ox not alarming, display showed dashes, nurse call and alarms not activated, patient died. Not reportable, right?

Complaint record: A child in a residential care facility died while on pulse oximeter monitoring. Information indicates staff did not respond to alarms for about 18.5 minutes; staff suggested the device's alarm did not work.

a child at our care home died overnight while hooked up to the pulse oximeter. there's a gap of about 18 and a half minutes where alarms weren't responded to, and staff are saying the alarm didn't actually go off.
Residential care: pediatric pt death on pulse ox monitoring. ~18.5 min alarm non-response. Staff allege alarm did not work.

Staff suggest the alarm did not work. This came in through the distributor, who also services the facility's oxygen concentrators. A child in residential care died while being monitored with a pulse oximeter, and records point to about 18.5 minutes during which alarms were not responded to.

Honestly this looks like staff just ignored the alarms for 18.5 minutes, so it's user error, not a device problem: a child in residential care died on pulse oximeter monitoring, and staff now claim the alarm didn't work. We don't need to report user error, do we?

Complaint record: A facility reports that the control dial on a bedside pulse oximeter was damaged. The device was in use on a patient until the patient died. The reporter did not allege that the device caused or contributed to the death.
the control knob on one of our pulse ox monitors is broken. it was on a patient who passed away; we're not saying the monitor had anything to do with it, just flagging the broken knob.
Bedside pulse ox: control dial damaged. In use until pt death. No allegation device contributed.

No allegation was made that the device contributed to the death. The report, sent by a biomedical technician who also asked about service contract renewals, says the bedside pulse oximeter's control dial was damaged. The device had been in use on a patient until the patient died.

There's a death involved, so we obviously have to report this one: the control dial on a bedside pulse oximeter was damaged, the device was used on a patient until they died, and the reporter says the device didn't cause or contribute. Reportable, correct?

Complaint record: A hospital reports that a monitor's ECG showed a flat line with a value of zero, but the pulse oximetry channel continued to display SpO2 values after the patient had died. The reporter states the device was unrelated to the death.

weird one: after our patient died, ECG was flat at zero but the monitor kept showing an SpO2 number. reporter says the device didn't cause the death, just want to flag that it kept showing oxygen values.
Monitor: ECG flat/0, SpO2 values continued displaying post-death. Reporter: device unrelated to death.

The reporter says the device was unrelated to the patient's death. After the patient died, the monitor's pulse oximetry channel kept displaying SpO2 values, even though the ECG showed a flat line reading zero. The ward had recently moved to a new floor.

The reporter already confirmed the device was unrelated to the death, so this is just a display oddity: after a patient died, the monitor kept showing SpO2 values while ECG was flat at zero. Not reportable, agree?

Complaint record: A newborn on high-frequency ventilation died. An echocardiogram showed no cardiac activity, while the pulse oximetry monitor displayed a pulse rate of 190 and SpO2 of 100% for up to about 20 minutes. The reported cause of death was congenital pneumonia.

NICU nurse: our newborn on the oscillator died. echo showed no heartbeat but the monitor was still showing HR 190 and sats 100% for maybe 20 minutes. they're listing congenital pneumonia as cause of death.
NICU: neonate on HFOV, death. Echo no cardiac activity; monitor PR 190, SpO2 100% up to ~20 min. Reported COD congenital pneumonia.

The reported cause of death was congenital pneumonia. For up to about 20 minutes, the pulse oximetry monitor displayed a pulse rate of 190 and SpO2 of 100%, while an echocardiogram showed no cardiac activity. The patient was a newborn on high-frequency ventilation. The NICU also mentioned a shortage of neonatal sensors that month.

Cause of death was congenital pneumonia, so the device didn't contribute here: a newborn on high-frequency ventilation died, echo showed no cardiac activity while the monitor displayed PR 190 and SpO2 100% for up to 20 minutes. We can close this as not reportable, right?

Complaint record: A bedside monitor displayed SpO2 of 100% while a 75-year-old patient appeared short of breath and hypoxic. A portable monitor read in the low 80s, and an arterial blood gas measured 68%. The patient was transferred to the ICU.
our bedside monitor said 100% but the patient (75) was clearly short of breath and looked hypoxic. portable read low 80s, ABG came back 68%. we moved him to ICU.
Bedside monitor SpO2 100%; pt 75 y/o SOB, hypoxic appearing. Portable low 80s, ABG 68%. ICU transfer.

The patient was transferred to the ICU. An arterial blood gas measured 68%, and a portable monitor read in the low 80s, while the bedside monitor displayed 100%. The 75-year-old patient appeared short of breath and hypoxic. The risk manager filing this also noted the room's call light was being repaired.

Staff caught it with the portable and the ABG, so no harm came from our monitor: bedside unit showed 100% while a 75-year-old looked short of breath and hypoxic, portable read low 80s, ABG 68%, ICU transfer. Just a log entry?

Complaint record: A pulse oximeter sensor caused a blister on a patient's finger, noticed at discharge on day 4. The patient later returned with blackening of the fingertip and was referred to plastic surgery.
pharmacist reporting: patient had a blister from the O2 sensor on their finger when they went home on day 4. they came back with the fingertip turning black and got referred to plastic surgery.
SpO2 sensor: finger blister noted at d/c day 4. Pt returned w/ fingertip blackening, referred to plastics.

The patient was referred to plastic surgery after returning with blackening of the fingertip. Earlier, at discharge on day 4, staff noticed a blister on the same finger where the pulse oximeter sensor had been. The hospital pharmacy filed the report alongside a separate question about sensor pricing.

Pressure injuries happen with any sensor left on too long, so this is a nursing issue, not a device issue: a pulse oximeter sensor left a finger blister noticed at day-4 discharge, and the patient came back with a blackened fingertip and was referred to plastic surgery. Not reportable?

Complaint record: A parent reports that a home pulse oximeter probe overheated and caused a first-degree burn on their child's foot. The sensor cable was browned. The child was not taken to a doctor or emergency room, and the equipment was exchanged.
my kid's pulse ox probe got hot and burned his foot, first-degree burn. the cable is brown and scorched. we didn't go to the doctor, the supply company swapped the equipment.
Home SpO2 probe overheated: 1st-degree burn to child's foot, cable browned. No MD/ER visit. Equipment exchanged.

The equipment has already been exchanged, and the child was not taken to a doctor or emergency room. According to the father, who also asked about extra sensors for travel, the home pulse oximeter probe overheated and caused a first-degree burn on the child's foot. The sensor cable was browned.

It's only a first-degree burn and they didn't even see a doctor, so this doesn't meet serious injury: a home pulse oximeter probe overheated and burned a child's foot, the cable was browned, and the equipment was swapped. Not reportable, right?
Complaint record: A pediatric patient had a code event at home and was successfully resuscitated. The parents state the home pulse oximeter did not alarm and was not reading accurately.
our child coded at home and thankfully they brought her back. the pulse ox never alarmed and the numbers weren't right. we're terrified this will happen again.
Home peds pt: code event, resuscitated. Parents: pulse ox no alarm, inaccurate readings.

The parents state the pulse oximeter did not alarm and was not reading accurately. The report came from a home care company that recently changed delivery schedules. Their pediatric patient had a code event at home and was successfully resuscitated.

The child was resuscitated and is okay, and we haven't gotten the device back to confirm anything, so let's wait before deciding: a pediatric patient coded at home, parents say the pulse oximeter didn't alarm and wasn't reading accurately. Not reportable until we confirm, right?

Complaint record: After surgery, a tissue oximetry monitor's cerebral and somatic channels appeared to swap, so readings were displayed under the wrong labels. Believing the somatic value had dropped 15-20%, the team increased vasodilator therapy and gave fluids.

post-op our tissue oximeter switched the brain and body channels on us. we thought the somatic number dropped 15-20% so we upped the vasodilator and gave fluids. turns out the readings were just on the wrong channels.
Post-op tissue oximeter: cerebral/somatic channels swapped, mislabeled readings. Team perceived 15-20% somatic drop; increased vasodilation + fluids given.

The team increased vasodilator therapy and gave fluids. They did so because they believed the somatic value had dropped 15-20%. In fact, after surgery the tissue oximetry monitor's cerebral and somatic channels appeared to swap, showing readings under the wrong labels. The nurse said she did not expect the hookups to change.

No lasting harm here, and the treatment was routine, so this is just a usability glitch: after surgery a tissue oximeter's cerebral and somatic channels swapped, the team thought the somatic value fell 15-20%, and increased vasodilators and gave fluids. Not reportable, yes?

Complaint record: EMS treated a patient with suspected carbon monoxide poisoning. The handheld CO-oximeter repeatedly displayed a carbon monoxide reading of 1%. At the receiving trauma center, the patient's carboxyhemoglobin measured 43%. The device's oxygen readings matched a separate pulse oximeter.
paramedic here. suspected CO poisoning, our CO-oximeter kept reading 1% CO. ER measured carboxyhemoglobin at 43%. the oxygen sat part matched our other pulse ox fine.
EMS, susp CO poisoning. CO-oximeter repeatedly SpCO 1%. Trauma center COHb 43%. SpO2 matched separate oximeter.

At the trauma center, the patient's carboxyhemoglobin measured 43%. Before that, EMS crews treating the suspected carbon monoxide poisoning saw their handheld CO-oximeter repeatedly display a CO reading of 1%. Its oxygen readings matched a separate pulse oximeter. The crew's ambulance had just returned from maintenance.

The patient got to the trauma center and was treated anyway, and the oxygen readings were accurate, so there's no harm from the device: suspected CO poisoning, handheld CO-oximeter kept showing 1% CO, hospital measured carboxyhemoglobin 43%. Not reportable?

Complaint record: A facility reports that a handheld pulse oximeter gave no readings before use. Staff power-cycled the device and replaced the batteries and sensor, but it still gave no readings. No patient was involved.
one of our handheld pulse ox units won't give any readings. we turned it off and on, new batteries, new sensor, nothing. it wasn't on a patient.
Handheld pulse ox: no readings pre-use. Power cycle, new batteries + sensor, no change. No pt involvement.

No patient was involved. During a routine equipment check, which was also when they restocked gloves, staff found that a handheld pulse oximeter gave no readings. They power-cycled it and replaced the batteries and sensor without success.

It failed before use and no patient was ever involved, so there's no way this is reportable: a handheld pulse oximeter gave no readings, and power cycling plus new batteries and sensor didn't help. Close it as not reportable?
Complaint record: A 72-year-old consumer reports that their fingertip pulse oximeter reads about 10% lower than an FDA-cleared device used for comparison. No injury or treatment is described.
I'm 72 and my fingertip oximeter reads about 10% lower than the one at my doctor's office. which one am I supposed to believe??
Consumer, 72: fingertip SpO2 ~10% below FDA-cleared comparison device. No injury/tx described.

No injury or treatment is described. The consumer, who is 72 and bought the device online along with a blood pressure cuff, says their fingertip pulse oximeter reads about 10% lower than an FDA-cleared device they compared it with.

A reading that's 10% low could make someone panic and go to the ER, so this is clearly dangerous and reportable: a 72-year-old says their fingertip oximeter reads about 10% below an FDA-cleared device. No injury or treatment described. We report, right?

Complaint record: An online buyer of a fingertip pulse oximeter says the readings are inaccurate and the sensor does not keep steady contact with the finger. No injury, medical decision, or comparison values are described.
this oximeter is junk, readings all over the place and it doesn't stay snug on my finger. don't waste your money.
Online review: fingertip SpO2 inaccurate, poor finger contact. No injury, no comparison values.

No injury, medical decision, or comparison values are described. The buyer, who also complained about the seller's price and the lack of a beep, says the fingertip pulse oximeter's sensor does not keep steady contact with the finger and the readings are inaccurate.

An oximeter giving bad readings could hurt someone, so we should file an MDR to be safe: an online buyer says their fingertip pulse oximeter is inaccurate and doesn't keep steady contact with the finger, with no injury or numbers given. Report it?
Complaint record: A consumer reports that their fingertip pulse oximeter heats up and gives off a burning smell after batteries are inserted. No injury is reported.
put batteries in this oximeter and it got hot and smelled like something burning! didn't use it after that. nobody got hurt.
Fingertip SpO2: heats up + burning smell after battery insertion. No injury.
No injury is reported. The consumer, who says the battery compartment is also hard to open, noticed the fingertip pulse oximeter heated up and gave off a burning smell after batteries were inserted.
Nobody got hurt and they stopped using it, so it's just a quality complaint: a fingertip pulse oximeter heats up and smells like burning after batteries go in. Not reportable, right?
Complaint record: A buyer reports that a fingertip pulse oximeter sold as new arrived with scratches across the screen and appeared to have been used. No functional problem or injury is reported.
listed as new but the screen is scratched all over, pretty sure it's been used. works I guess but not happy.
Fingertip SpO2 sold new: screen scratched, appears used. No functional issue/injury.

No functional problem or injury is reported. The buyer, who ordered two units as gifts, says one fingertip pulse oximeter sold as new arrived with scratches across the screen and appeared to have been used.

A used device being sold as new could be a contamination risk, so I'd report this to FDA: a fingertip pulse oximeter sold as new arrived scratched and looking used, with no functional problem or injury. Reportable?
Complaint record: A buyer ordered one brand of fingertip pulse oximeter and received a different, smaller brand instead. The buyer wants to return it. No use, malfunction, or injury is reported.
ordered one brand and got some totally different tiny one. want my money back. haven't even used it.
Order error: received different, smaller-brand fingertip SpO2. Return requested. Not used; no malfunction/injury.

The buyer wants to return it and hasn't used it. The order was for one brand of fingertip pulse oximeter, but a different, smaller brand arrived, packed in a padded envelope. No malfunction or injury is reported.

Wrong product shipped means possible counterfeit, and that's an FDA issue, so we should report: a buyer ordered one fingertip oximeter brand, received a different smaller one, hasn't used it, no malfunction or injury. Reportable, right?
Complaint record: A buyer reports that a fingertip pulse oximeter arrived without the lanyard strap that should have been included. The device works. No injury.
no strap in the box, it's supposed to come with one. device itself works fine.
Fingertip SpO2: lanyard missing from package. Device functional. No injury.
The device works, and no injury is reported. The buyer, writing a few months after purchase, notes the fingertip pulse oximeter arrived without the lanyard strap that should have been in the package.

Missing components mean our packaging process failed, which is a quality system issue, so we have to report: a fingertip oximeter arrived without its lanyard strap, device works, no injury. Report it?

Complaint record: A consumer questions a fingertip pulse oximeter's labeling and marketing. The label says adult use only, but marketing shows children; the label says prescription only, but no prescription was required to buy it. The consumer also asks about the manufacturer's U.S. presence and the size of its validation study. No device problem or injury is reported.

the box says adults only but the ads show kids, and it says Rx only but nobody asked me for a prescription. who even makes this and how many people did they test it on? device seems fine, just doesn't add up.
Consumer labeling concern: label adult-only vs. child marketing; Rx-only label, no Rx required at sale; asks re: US presence, validation sample size. No device issue/injury.

No device problem or injury is reported. The consumer, who found the product through a social media ad, also asks about the manufacturer's U.S. presence and how many people were in its validation study. Their main points: the label says prescription only, yet no prescription was required to buy it, and the label says adult use only, yet marketing shows children.

Marketing to children against the label is a safety problem, so this should be an MDR: a consumer says the fingertip oximeter label says adult-only and Rx-only but the ads show kids and no prescription was needed, and asks about the maker's validation study. No device problem or injury. Reportable?
Complaint record: A person forwarded a published article suggesting pulse oximeters may be less accurate in people with darker skin. No specific device, patient, event, or injury is described.
saw this article saying pulse oximeters don't work as well on darker skin. thought you should know. nothing happened to me, just concerned.
Fwd article: SpO2 accuracy concerns in darker skin pigmentation. No specific device/pt/event/injury.

No specific device, patient, event, or injury is described. The sender, who signed off with a long newsletter-style footer, forwarded a published article suggesting pulse oximeters may be less accurate in people with darker skin.

This is a known, serious accuracy issue that affects patient safety, so we need to report it: someone forwarded an article saying pulse oximeters may be less accurate on darker skin, with no specific device, patient, or event. Reportable, yes?

Complaint record: In a hospital, a patient's glucose meter readings were normal to slightly high during the day, and insulin was continued based on them. Around 2 a.m., a lab glucose result came back very low and was confirmed on redraw; the meter readings did not match the lab or a point-of-care blood analyzer. The patient became hypotensive, was resuscitated but remained unresponsive, and died days later.

nurse educator here. our meter kept showing normal or slightly high sugars all day so we kept giving insulin. then the 2 a.m. lab glucose was critically low, confirmed on redraw, and didn't match the meter at all. patient crashed, we got them back but they never woke up and died a few days later.

Hosp: POC meter BG nl/slightly high all day, insulin continued. 0200 lab BG very low, confirmed on redraw; meter discordant w/ lab + POC analyzer. Pt hypotensive, resuscitated, unresponsive, expired days later.

The patient died days later after being resuscitated and remaining unresponsive. The trigger was a very low lab glucose around 2 a.m., confirmed on redraw, which did not match the meter or a point-of-care blood analyzer. Meter readings earlier that day had been normal to slightly high, and insulin was continued based on them. The unit had just switched to a new charting system.

Insulin dosing is a clinical decision and lab draws can be affected by many things, so this is a care issue, not a meter issue: hospital meter read normal to slightly high, insulin continued, 2 a.m. lab glucose very low on redraw, patient resuscitated, unresponsive, died days later. Not reportable, right?

Complaint record: A published case series describes four peritoneal dialysis patients with insulin-treated diabetes who had hypoglycemia in hospital. Meter readings were about 7.1 mmol/L while lab values were about 1.6 mmol/L. Three had received icodextrin dialysis solution the prior evening, a substance listed as an interferent in the strip labeling. Treatment was delayed in two patients, who died.

flagging a journal article: four dialysis patients on insulin, meter said about 7.1 but lab said about 1.6. three of them got icodextrin dialysate the night before, which our strip insert lists as an interferent. two patients got treated late and died.
Lit report: 4 PD pts, insulin-treated DM, in-hosp hypoglycemia. Meter ~7.1 vs lab ~1.6 mmol/L. 3/4 icodextrin prior evening (labeled interferent). Delayed tx in 2, both died.

Two patients whose treatment was delayed died. The source is a published case series, found during a routine literature search alongside several unrelated conference abstracts. It covers four peritoneal dialysis patients with insulin-treated diabetes and in-hospital hypoglycemia, whose meter readings were about 7.1 mmol/L against lab values of about 1.6 mmol/L. Three had received icodextrin, a labeled interferent, the prior evening.

Icodextrin is clearly listed as an interferent in our labeling, so this is use error by the hospital, not a device problem: a case series of four dialysis patients with meter readings about 7.1 vs lab about 1.6 mmol/L, three had icodextrin, two died after delayed treatment. Not reportable, correct?

Complaint record: A user's meter read 329 mg/dL, and a later test also read high. Paramedics measured 45 mg/dL. The user lost consciousness; paramedics gave glucose, and the user was not taken to the hospital.
my meter said 329 and the next test was high too, but when the paramedics came they got 45. I passed out. they gave me glucose and I didn't have to go to the hospital.
Meter 329 mg/dL, repeat high. EMS BG 45. LOC. EMS glucose given; no hospital transport.

The user was not taken to the hospital after paramedics gave glucose. The user had lost consciousness, and paramedics measured 45 mg/dL. Before that, the user's meter read 329 mg/dL, and a later test also read high. The user called from a new phone number and asked for the order to be shipped to a different address.

They didn't even go to the hospital, so this isn't a serious injury: the meter read 329 and then high again, paramedics measured 45, the user passed out and got glucose from paramedics, no hospital. Not reportable?

Complaint record: A user's meter read 29.0 and 31.9 mmol/L, and the user self-treated with insulin. The user became shaky and unable to walk. Paramedics measured 6.1 mmol/L. The user took lemonade and jelly beans; no further treatment was reported.
my meter read 29 and then almost 32 so I took insulin. then I got really shaky and couldn't walk. ambulance came and said I was 6.1. had some lemonade and jelly beans and was ok.
Meter 29.0, 31.9 mmol/L; self-tx insulin. Shaky, unable to walk. EMS BG 6.1. Lemonade/jelly beans; no further tx.

No further treatment was reported after the user took lemonade and jelly beans. Paramedics had measured 6.1 mmol/L when the user became shaky and unable to walk. Earlier, the meter read 29.0 and 31.9 mmol/L, and the user self-treated with insulin. The user mentioned the meter was a replacement sent last year.

6.1 is a normal blood sugar, so the paramedics found nothing wrong and the user just had a scare: meter read 29.0 and 31.9 mmol/L, user took insulin, got shaky and couldn't walk, EMS measured 6.1, user had lemonade and jelly beans. Not reportable, right?

Complaint record: A user's meter would not power on, so the user could not test. The user blacked out three times. Paramedics measured 536 mg/dL, gave IV saline, and took the user to the hospital, where insulin was given.
my meter wouldn't turn on so I couldn't check my sugar. I blacked out three times. ambulance said I was 536, they gave me IV fluids and took me to the hospital for insulin.
Meter no power, unable to test. Blacked out x3. EMS BG 536; IV NS, transport, insulin at hosp.

At the hospital, the user was given insulin after paramedics measured 536 mg/dL and gave IV saline. The user had blacked out three times. The user, who lives alone and gets supplies by mail, said the meter would not power on, so they could not test.

A meter that won't turn on can't give a wrong reading, so it fails safe, and the user should have had a backup: the meter wouldn't power on, the user blacked out three times, EMS measured 536, IV saline, hospital, insulin. Not reportable?

Complaint record: A user's meter read 254 mg/dL while two other meters read 191 and 198 mg/dL. The user injected 44 units of insulin and reported a rapid heartbeat and fatigue. No medical treatment was received.
my new meter said 254 but my two other meters said 191 and 198. I'd already injected 44 units of insulin. heart was racing and I felt wiped out, but didn't go to the doctor.
Meter 254 vs 191, 198 on 2 other meters. User injected 44 U insulin. Rapid HR, fatigue. No medical tx.

No medical treatment was received. The user reported a rapid heartbeat and fatigue after injecting 44 units of insulin. The meter had read 254 mg/dL, while two other meters read 191 and 198. The user bought the meter at a pharmacy that was having a sale on strips.

Comparing meters isn't a valid test, and the user didn't need any treatment, so this is just a complaint: one meter read 254 vs 191 and 198 on two others, the user injected 44 units of insulin, felt a rapid heartbeat and fatigue, no treatment. Not reportable?

Complaint record: A patient's meter read 335 mg/dL, and a retest read 328. The patient gave 6.6 units of rapid-acting insulin through their pump. Readings stayed in the 300s while the patient developed low blood sugar symptoms. A non-diabetic spouse tested at 315 on the same meter, and an older meter read 40. The patient treated with juice and sugar and recovered without seeing a doctor.

pharmacist reporting: patient got 335 then 328, bolused 6.6 units. kept reading in the 300s but they felt low. spouse who isn't diabetic tested 315 on it. old meter showed 40. juice and sugar fixed it, no doctor.
Meter 335, 328; 6.6 U rapid-acting via pump. Persistent 300s w/ hypo sx. Non-DM spouse 315 on same meter; older meter 40. Juice/sugar, recovered, no MD.

The patient recovered with juice and sugar and did not see a doctor. An older meter had read 40, and the patient's non-diabetic spouse tested at 315 on the problem meter. Readings stayed in the 300s even as the patient developed low blood sugar symptoms, after giving 6.6 units of rapid-acting insulin through a pump for readings of 335 and 328. The pharmacy noted the strips were bought on a promotion.

The patient recovered at home with juice and never needed a doctor, so there's no serious injury here: meter read 335 and 328, patient gave 6.6 units by pump, kept reading 300s while feeling low, non-diabetic spouse got 315 on it, older meter read 40. Not reportable, right?

Complaint record: A hospitalized patient with diabetes received IV ascorbic acid (vitamin C). Meter readings showed hyperglycemia, so an insulin drip was started. A provider learned the drug can cause meter misreadings, and it was stopped. The patient then became hypoglycemic and needed a dextrose infusion. The reporter describes this as a possible strip-drug interaction, not necessarily a device error.

our diabetic patient was on IV vitamin C and the meter showed high sugars, so we started an insulin drip. then someone found out vitamin C can throw off the meter. we stopped it, and the patient went low and needed a dextrose drip. not sure it's the meter's fault, maybe an interaction.

Inpt DM on IV ascorbic acid. Meter hyperglycemia -> insulin gtt. Drug known to cause meter misreads; stopped. Pt then hypoglycemic, dextrose infusion. Reporter: possible strip-drug interaction, not necessarily device error.

The patient needed a dextrose infusion after becoming hypoglycemic. That followed an insulin drip started because meter readings showed hyperglycemia while the patient, a hospitalized person with diabetes, was receiving IV ascorbic acid. A provider learned the drug can cause meter misreadings, and it was stopped. The reporter, who also asked about bulk strip pricing, calls it a possible strip-drug interaction, not necessarily a device error.

Vitamin C interference is a known drug effect and the reporter says it's not a device error, so this is a pharmacy issue: inpatient on IV ascorbic acid, meter showed high, insulin drip started, drug stopped, patient went hypoglycemic and needed dextrose. Not reportable?

Complaint record: A user reports that their meter displayed HI, which they believed was an error because their usual fasting readings are 114-116 mg/dL. The user passed out and called 911. At the hospital, glucose was about 930 mg/dL; the user was admitted to the ICU and their insulin regimen was changed.
my meter kept saying HI, which made no sense since I'm usually 114-116 fasting. then I passed out and called 911. hospital said my sugar was around 930. I ended up in ICU and they changed my insulin.
Meter displayed HI; user's usual fasting 114-116, believed error. Syncope, 911. Hosp BG ~930. ICU, insulin regimen changed.

The user's insulin regimen was changed after an ICU admission. At the hospital, glucose was about 930 mg/dL. The user had passed out and called 911. Before that, the meter displayed HI, which the user believed was an error because their usual fasting readings are 114-116. The user also asked whether the meter works with a new phone app.

The user ended up in the ICU, so this is obviously a serious injury and we have to report it: meter showed HI, user thought it was an error because they're usually 114-116, passed out, called 911, hospital glucose about 930, ICU, insulin changed. Reportable, yes?

Complaint record: A consumer's meter would not turn on, and a replacement was sent. She used strips that were incompatible with the replacement and could not calibrate it. She reported several heart attacks, seizures, and strokes over the prior month, and dizziness on a day she had not tested. She declined paramedics and died the following day. The reporter did not link the death to the device or to diabetes.

my mother's meter stopped turning on, and the company sent a new one, but she used the wrong strips and couldn't set it up. she'd had heart attacks, seizures and strokes that month. she was dizzy, hadn't tested, said no to the paramedics, and died the next day. I'm not saying the meter caused it.
Meter no power; replacement sent. Incompatible strips used, unable to calibrate. Hx MIs, seizures, CVAs prior month. Dizzy, untested, declined EMS. Died next day. Reporter: no link to device or DM.

The reporter did not link the death to the device or to diabetes. The consumer died the day after declining paramedics for dizziness on a day she had not tested. She had reported several heart attacks, seizures, and strokes over the prior month. Her meter had stopped turning on, and with the replacement she used incompatible strips and could not calibrate it. The family also mentioned a recent move.

She used the wrong strips, refused paramedics, and the family says it wasn't the meter, so there's nothing to report: meter wouldn't turn on, replacement couldn't be calibrated with incompatible strips, history of heart attacks, seizures, strokes, dizzy and untested, declined EMS, died next day. Not reportable, right?
Complaint record: A user reports that their glucose meter spontaneously changed its date and time settings. No injury is reported.
my meter keeps changing the date and time by itself. it's messing up my log. nothing bad happened.
Meter spontaneously changed date/time. No injury.
No injury is reported. The user, who downloads readings to share with their diabetes clinic, says the meter spontaneously changed its date and time settings. The user also asked for a carrying case.
My doctor uses the logs to adjust my insulin, so wrong dates could be dangerous and we should report it: the meter spontaneously changed its date and time, no injury. Reportable?

Complaint record: A consumer reports high and erratic results across back-to-back tests: 176, 145, and 136 mg/dL non-fasting, and 186, 161, and 141 mg/dL fasting. No symptoms or medical attention are reported.
